title: Breaking And Entering: Ripple Effect Band On The Importance Of Storytelling
summary: Ripple Effect Band members Jodie Kell and Rachel Thomas stopped by the studio to talk with Lauren and Simon about songwriting in the now-endangered language of their people, their home on Arnhem Land and how they came to be the critically acclaimed all woman rock band.
transcript:
Rachel Thomas and Jodie Kell of Ripple Effect Band joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 1 May 2025, the day after the band performed at the APRA Music Awards. They discussed their debut album Mayawa, the band's beginnings in Maningrida, and the connections between language, country and song.

Simon: As Lauren mentioned, it's such a huge honour and a thrill for us to have you with us today. For any listeners coming to Triple R that haven't encountered your music so regularly, we did want to give a little bit of an introduction and context. Ripple Effect Band are a groundbreaking group in so many ways, from the remote community of Maningrida in West Arnhem Land, Northern Territory. You’re the first women from your community to form a band, bringing together a very distinctive, what's been described as saltwater rock sound, blending reggae and blues, and, of course, deeply rooted in your connection to country. A central tenet of your work is the use of multiple languages, including the highly endangered Na-kara. The music is not only a beautiful source of enrichment, but also an act of cultural preservation and revitalisation. Amidst all of that, you were playing the APRA Awards last night. We saw some great videos, including, I think, you were covering King Stingray, 'Through The Trees'. Can you tell us a little bit more about your experience at the APRA Awards last night?

Rachel: It was good last night, and there were too many at the front. [Unclear audio at 00:05:29–00:05:34] But it's difficult. They're different to us. They're from East Arnhem. [Unclear audio at 00:05:42–00:05:44]

Simon: It would have been an extraordinary experience. We did want to talk to you a little bit about the impact that your music has. There are so many beautiful stories that you're sharing and important themes that you're exploring. In a live music context, it's quite special as well. What do you hope that people feel or take away when they're seeing you perform?

Jodie: I think we love performing live and sharing the music. I think there's something special about seeing the women playing on the instruments and singing live. Last night when we performed, like Rachel was saying, King Stingray are from East Arnhem and also they're men. The women are from West Arnhem, and women. We did things like we switched around in the middle section when they were singing what they call manikay or bunggul, traditional. We can't sing that as women. Rachel had a beautiful song that she'd written, which was about the sunset.

Rachel: It's all about the story that I'm sitting up the cliff and watching the sun going down. I turn around and look at the rain coming toward us, and in the ocean I can see the lightning striking. So it's all about my language.

Jodie: It's like a traditional kun-borrk feeling to it. It's different but the same. To see that live, a lot of people last night afterwards were saying that they could feel this deep meaning in the music because of the way we're performing, and how it meant a lot to all of us to have that chance to sing that big band King Stingray's songs, but change it up, and show respect to East Arnhem and show respect to West Arnhem, and the connections, and yet the difference as well.

Host: We'd love to go back to the start as well. How did Ripple Effect Band first come together?

Guest: What a long time ago, when we were young ladies.

Jodie: I was in Maningrida. I went there in 2000 as a schoolteacher, teaching music in the high school. That was when the girls started learning, because there was myself, and there was Zeb Olsen, who's up in Castlemaine, and also Megan Atfield. So having women teachers was big. For me personally, a really important thing was I would sit on my front veranda at my house and I would hear this beautiful singing coming from next door. I got braver and braver, because I'd only just gone to move there, and so one day I walked around the fence and there was this lady and her husband, sitting very young and skinny. That was Rachel and her husband, singing beautiful gospel and also history songs like 'Makéddja', Turtle Song, Hunting Song.

Rachel: She heard us, me and my partner, we were singing. It's a cliff song. We were both sitting there, watching the island, and she heard us. [Unclear audio at 00:09:26–00:09:27] She came there to sit with us, myself and my partner.

Jodie: They opened their arms. I said, 'I want to learn,' and they just taught me everything. That was the beginning of a big friendship and music together. If you listen to our single of 'Walaya', not the one on the album, but the single we released, at the very beginning there's a recording that was done on a tape player of Rachel's partner singing that song. So we put that at the beginning. He's passed away now, so that's a tribute to him and that beautiful moment.

Host: There are beautiful tributes to family and community throughout the debut album Mayawa, which was released last year. It contains beautiful stories and recordings. Perhaps we could talk about one in particular, Rachel. That's the story of Cyclone Monica, which we understand also includes your mother's voice as part of that recording. Could you share a little bit about the significance of this story and what it was like recording it?

Rachel: My mum, she used to tell all about spirit dreaming. It's called Djómi. People come from other places, she go out to the barge landing or in the sacred site to start calling out for the Djómi, spirit Djómi. [Unclear audio at 00:11:02–00:11:06] So she can sing out and they will look after them, those people. [Unclear audio at 00:11:09–00:11:12]

Host: The album itself, Mayawa, we understand the title translates to, is it beach or coast in Na-kara? There are lots of stories which relate to this particular region. Can you tell us more about how the name reflects the spirit of the album?

Guest: We spend a lot of time at the beach. [Unclear audio at 00:11:40–00:11:44] We love fishing and hunting. Maningrida is on the coast, on the mouth of the Liverpool River. When you head out of town on the dirt road, you can head towards Darwin or you take a left, and then you go along there and you can go to all these places like Makórrdja, Ndjúdda. Makórrdja looks back to Maningrida, and then you come around the point to Ndjúdda, which is beautiful.

Guest: It goes round and round, from Nardilmuk to Ndjúdda, Makórrdja. And the other way, keep going, Nardilmuk to Rocky Point. Berraja, all the way.

Guest: We spend a lot of time along that. You might go, 'Let's go to Rocky Point. We'll go to dinner camp, we'll go fishing there,' or, 'Let's go to Ndjúdda, get some wengala,' or Makórrdja to get crab. There's lots of crab.

Guest: We don't go to the beach and lie around in our [Unclear audio at 00:12:48–00:12:50]. It's too much to do. It's a time when you're out and you're hunting, and we sit around the fire and we sing songs and we think about all the old people and all the history, and tell stories. In naming the album, we spoke with Rona and her grandmother and we said we'd like to name it for those times spent out on the country.

Host: Ripple Effect Band sing in multiple languages, especially the endangered Na-kara language, which we were speaking about earlier. That's been very central to your identity. Can you tell us a bit more about that aspect of the group, the importance of weaving language through song?

Rachel: We speak Ndjébbana.

Jodie: So the Ndjébbana language that Rachel speaks, it's connected to the country. When you sing about country, you sing in language.

Guest: We sing Ndjébbana, we sing Na-kara, we sing Burarra and Kune. Kune is inland, so that's freshwater country. We are the saltwater country.

Guest: When we sing, say, 'Cyclone', because 'Cyclone' is about Maningrida, which is the Dhukurrdji clan, Dhukurrdji land, part of the Ndjébbana language group, you sing in that language. Then when you sing about 'Na-meyarra', which is Na-kara land, you sing in that language. So the language connects to the country and it connects to the stories. [Unclear audio at 00:15:05–00:15:09]

Host: It's so wonderful to hear more about the nature of the music that you're making and the impact that you're having. The band itself, Ripple Effect Band, really contains that idea of the influence and the impact that you're having. Could we ask a little bit about the effects of your music that you're seeing on the community in Maningrida and beyond?

Jodie: I think when I was in Maningrida just around Easter, I saw the school bus going past and they were playing 'Na-kalamandjarda' out of the school bus. It's important for all the children. They love singing, they like singing [Unclear audio at 00:15:56–00:15:58], and they love singing in language. 'Cyclone' song, we performed it, well, we didn't perform it. We worked with a big school event in Sydney, so 400 schoolchildren sang 'Cyclone' at the Sydney Opera House, with a string ensemble and piano. When we did that, it was so exciting that then the school organised that the whole school then sang the same version with the recorded violins. Rachel was there and all the [Unclear audio at 00:16:38–00:16:40] mob were there too, like David Jones and the traditional landowners.

What were they doing? Did they like it?

Rachel: [Unclear audio at 00:16:45–00:16:52] My auntie, she loved that Monica Cyclone song.

Host: How did it feel for you to see?

Rachel: It also reminds me about my mum. [Unclear audio at 00:17:03–00:17:13] Because she knows all the Djómi spirit running away and then still coming back again. I'm really proud for my song about Monica Cyclone, from where I come from, Maningrida, called Dhukurrdji.

Host: We've actually lined up a special version that you recorded live for us at Triple R, of 'Cyclone', when you were here in the performance space towards the end of last year for that very special show. We did want to find out, are you working on some new material? What's next for Ripple Effect Band?

Guest: Seeing that we love Triple R so much, I might just say there may be a single coming out soon. We haven't fully announced it yet, but keep your ears posted. Of course, we'll let you all know. We did a bit of recording in Castlemaine last year while we were down. Then we've got ideas for a new album. We've been singing lots of different songs, thinking about Patricia's new song, 'Hunting Song'. We have one that we've been thinking about all the travelling that we do and all the different places we go and share music, and how fun that is. So I reckon a new album is in the works, but definitely a new song. There you go, I've said it now. Surprise.

Host: We cannot wait. Rachel and Jodie from Ripple Effect Band, thank you so much for dropping by and joining us on Breaking and Entering today.
